Two things are asked: **how big** the force is, and **what exerts it**.
**Step 1 — find the acceleration.** From rest to v in 2 s with uniform acceleration:
a = (v - 0)/2 = **v/2**, directed **east**.
**Step 2 — find the net force.**
F = ma = **mv/2**, eastward.
**Step 3 — ask which body exerts it.** The engine is **inside** the car. Internal forces
cannot accelerate the system that contains them; by Newton's third law they cancel in
pairs. The car can only be accelerated by an **external** force.
**Step 4 — identify that external force.** The engine turns the wheels, the tyres push
**backward** on the road, and the road pushes the tyres **forward** - that reaction is
**friction from the road** ✓ It is the only external horizontal force here, so it must be
the one of size mv/2.
**The test of it.** On sheet ice the engine works just as hard and the wheels spin, yet
the car does not accelerate - because the road cannot supply the friction ✓ That shows
plainly that the accelerating force comes from the **road**, not the engine.
**What the engine really does.** It supplies the **torque** that makes the tyres press
backward on the road, so it sets up the friction. But the force on the car is exerted by
the road.
**Reading the distractors.** "mv/2 exerted by the engine" ✗ has the magnitude right and
the agent wrong. "More than mv/2 ... overcomes friction" ✗ confuses driving friction with
resistive friction; the **net** force is exactly ma = mv/2 whatever the losses.
∴ mv/2 eastward, due to the friction on the tyres exerted by the road.

Escaping air carries momentum away, and the rate at which momentum leaves is the force.
**Step 1 — find the rate of mass loss.** 8 g = **8 x 10⁻³ kg** escapes in 5·6 s:
dm/dt = 8 x 10⁻³/5·6 = **1·43 x 10⁻³ kg s⁻¹**
**Step 2 — use the thrust equation.** Air leaving at speed u gives
F = u (dm/dt)
with u = 7 cm/s = **0·07 m s⁻¹**:
F = 0·07 x 1·43 x 10⁻³
= **1 x 10⁻⁴ N** ✓
**Why force = u dm/dt.** Each second a mass dm/dt leaves carrying momentum u(dm/dt). Force
is rate of change of momentum, so that product **is** the force - the same formula that
gives a rocket its thrust ✓ No acceleration term appears because the escaping air leaves
at a steady speed.
**A check on the size.** 10⁻⁴ N is about the weight of a **10 mg** grain - a tiny push,
which is right for a slow trickle of air from a pinhole ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **56 dyne** = 5·6 x 10⁻⁴ N ✗ comes from multiplying 8 x 7 and
mishandling the units. **10⁻² dyne** = 10⁻⁷ N ✗ and **10⁻⁶ N** ✗ are both far too small -
they follow from leaving the mass in grams or the speed in cm/s without converting ✓
**Where the unit care matters.** Convert **both** the mass to kg and the speed to m/s
before multiplying; doing one and not the other is exactly what the wrong options are
built from.
∴ 10⁻⁴ N.

Take moments about the end resting on the ground and the angle drops straight out.
**Step 1 — set up.** The bar has length L and weight **W** acting at its **mid-point**.
One end is on the ground, the other on the man's shoulder, the bar at angle θ.
**Step 2 — take moments about the ground end.** Let the shoulder push up with force R.
Measuring along the bar, the weight acts at L/2 and the shoulder at L, and both forces are
vertical, so each moment arm carries the same factor cos θ:
R (L cos θ) = W (L/2) cos θ
**Step 3 — cancel.** L and **cos θ** cancel from both sides:
**R = W/2** ✓
**Why the angle makes no difference.** Tilting the bar shortens **both** moment arms by
the same factor cos θ ✓ so the ratio of the two is unchanged. The man carries half the
weight whether the bar is nearly flat or steeply raised.
**The simpler way to see it.** The weight acts at the **centre**, exactly halfway between
the two supports. By symmetry the two supports share it equally: **W/2** each ✓
**A check on the ground reaction.** Vertical forces must balance:
N_ground + R = W, so N_ground = W − W/2 = **W/2** ✓ equal shares, as the symmetry demands.
**Reading the distractors.** **W sin θ** and **W cos θ** ✗ both make the load depend on
the tilt, which the cancellation rules out - and W cos θ would wrongly give the **full**
weight at θ = 0. **W** ✗ would mean the ground carried nothing, though one end plainly
rests on it ✓
**When would it not be W/2?** Only if the centre of gravity were **not** midway - a bar
thicker at one end would load the nearer support more. "Uniform heavy iron bar" is what
puts the centre in the middle.
∴ W/2.

At **constant speed** the motor's force balances weight plus friction exactly, and power
is that force times the speed.
**Step 1 — find the force needed.** Constant speed means zero acceleration, so the upward
pull T balances everything acting down:
T = mg + f
= (2000)(10) + 3000
= 20000 + 3000
= **23000 N**
**Step 2 — find the power.**
P = T v
= 23000 x 1·5
= **34500 W** ✓
**Why friction is added, not subtracted.** The lift moves **up**, so friction opposes it
and acts **down**, alongside the weight ✓ Both must be overcome. Had the lift been
descending, friction would help and the force would be 20000 − 3000.
**Why "minimum" power.** With no acceleration the motor does the least work that still
keeps the lift moving ✓ Any extra force would speed it up, and the question's constant
speed fixes the force at its smallest workable value.
**A check by energy rates.** Per second the lift rises 1·5 m, so
gain in potential energy: 20000 x 1·5 = **30000 J**
work against friction: 3000 x 1·5 = **4500 J**
total per second = **34500 W** ✓ the same figure, arrived at independently.
**Reading the distractors.** **23000** ✗ is the **force** in newtons, not the power - the
commonest slip, forgetting to multiply by v. **20000** ✗ is mg alone with friction
dropped. **23500** ✗ is 23000 + 500, an arithmetic trap.
**The formula to carry away.** For steady motion, **P = Fv**, with F the total resisting
force ✓
∴ 34500 W.

Work in the **frame of the accelerating wedge**, where the block is at rest and a
pseudo-force appears.
**Step 1 — list the forces in the wedge's frame.** For the block of mass m on the smooth
incline, which is accelerating horizontally with magnitude a:
**weight mg**, vertically down
**normal reaction N**, perpendicular to the incline
**pseudo-force ma**, horizontal, pointing **opposite** to the acceleration
Friction is absent - the surface is smooth, so N is the only contact force.
**Step 2 — resolve along the incline.** The block must stay at rest in this frame, so the
components along the slope balance:
mg sin α = ma cos α
**Step 3 — solve.**
a = g sin α/cos α
= **g tan α** ✓
**Step 4 — check with the perpendicular direction.** Resolving normal to the slope:
N = mg cos α + ma sin α
= mg cos α + mg tan α sin α
= mg(cos²α + sin²α)/cos α
= **mg sec α** ✓
a consistent, sensible value - larger than mg, as it must be when the wedge is also
pushing the block sideways.
**Why a pseudo-force is legitimate.** The wedge frame is **non-inertial**, and Newton's
laws hold in it only if every body is given an extra force −ma ✓ That is what converts a
moving problem into a statics problem.
**The ground-frame version, for comparison.** There the block really does accelerate
horizontally with a and not at all vertically:
horizontal: N sin α = ma
vertical: N cos α = mg
Dividing: **tan α = a/g**, so **a = g tan α** ✓ the same answer with no pseudo-force at
all - a good confirmation.
**Checking the limits.**
α → 0 (a flat floor): a = **0** ✓ no acceleration is needed to keep a block on level
ground from sliding.
α → 90° (a vertical wall): a → **∞** ✓ no finite acceleration can hold a block against a
smooth vertical wall, which is correct.
Only **g tan α** behaves this way, and that test alone eliminates the other three.
**Reading the distractors.**
**g** ✗ is independent of the angle, failing both limits above.
**g cosec α** ✗ and **g/tan α** ✗ both **blow up as α → 0**, predicting an infinite
acceleration to hold a block on a level floor - plainly wrong ✓
∴ a = g tan α.

Note: the printed key gives the third option, g cosec α. Both frames of reference give
mg sin α = ma cos α, hence a = g tan α, and the α → 0 limit rules out g cosec α outright.
The key has been corrected to the first option.
